doc.title: Arturo O'Farrill interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 6, 2024

title: What dance taught him about freedom and structure
summary: Working with Ballet Hispanico, Malpaso, Alvin Ailey and a San Francisco Ballet commission changed how he composes, seeing music as architecture and movement.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: dance. I started working with dance companies with Ballet Hispanico, Malpaso, Alvin Ailey. I just scored — I didn’t score, I was commissioned by the San Francisco Ballet Company to write a full ballet. I just had it premiered in the ballet at the War Memorial Opera House. And I find that my work with choreographers and dancers has revolutionized the way that I play, the way that I compose, the way that I — I now understand that for me music is architectural and visual. It’s not just notes and harmony. And I have to see notes moving like bodies, and I have to hear chords like choreography. And I have to have compositional structures that are architectural like a staged setting. And it really has freed me up. Here’s the essential mystery of music is that we are trying to capture freedom in amber. The composer is trying to capture the nuance of creation and set it down so that it can be replicated. That’s a dichotomy. That’s a real kind of a cross purposes, and so in a way one has to embrace the joy of codifying the moment of freedom if you will. A composer sits down to write or perform, a pianist sits down to play and hopes to come up with something that’s absolutely spontaneous in freedom and beautiful. But we’ve got the same ten fingers, the same twelve notes, and the same repeated patterns that we all are privy to. So in a way, the way that I’ve learned to kind of capture the freedom of living on both sides of ration and intuition is by looking at structure and finding that ballet — modern dance — is the ultimate expression of that living between ration and tuition. You can’t get 18 musicians to do the same thing unless it’s written down. But what you write down on paper has to come from a place of absolute spontaneity. How do you do that? How do you do that? And so I’ve found that one of the ways that I do it is by referencing all of my work output to dance. Those dancers have to do that. Dancers have to work very rigorously to realize their art because otherwise they’ll injure themselves. They’ll be bumping into one another. They’ll be falling. There’ll be mass mayhem, there’ll be broken bones. So in a way capturing that ineffable essence of freedom and instant spontaneous creation has to go through the process of codification. And so to me I’ve learned — from dance I’ve learned how to look at music as movement, as staging, as architecture, as absolute — and the beauty of flight. The beauty of flight. When you see a dancer jump up in the air and do a move that they’ve practiced a thousand times before, there is a moment at which they do have complete freedom. Now think about that mystery, about the mystery of doing something you’ve done a thousand times before and every time you do it it’s fresh and new and different in the slightest mechanism. Maybe the way you twirl your hand, maybe the way you come down on your feet, maybe the angle in which you — but that structure gives you the absolute key and entry point into freedom because you’re doing something you’ve done a thousand times before. You can play the blues the same way every single
day, or you can play the blues in a brand new miraculous fashion every single time and I think dance to me has given me some of that understanding.
